question: The shift towards digitally distributed video games and other digital media has created a troubling gap in consumer protection. Increasingly, video games are designed to depend on publisher-operated online servers to function, even when they contain single-player content.

When publishers decide to shut down these servers, consumers can lose access to products they have legally purchased, effectively rendering them unusable. Similar issues arise in relation to films and other digital media. This raises important questions about ownership, the preservation of digital content and consumer rights in the digital single market.

Consumers who purchase digital products should have a reasonable expectation that these products will remain usable or that alternative means of access will be provided if online services are discontinued. 1.
How does the Commission assess the compatibility of practices that render legally purchased digital games or other digital media permanently unusable with existing EU consumer protection legislation?

Is the Commission considering legislative or regulatory measures to ensure that publishers cannot deliberately disable access to digital products that consumers have purchased, including, where appropriate, by requiring offline functionality, server handover or other technical solutions?
How will the Commission ensure that consumers retain meaningful ownership of, and long-term access to, digital products that they have paid for?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026) EU consumer law does not set specific duration for the supply of digital content/service. Instead, Directive 2019/770/EU (DCD)1 requires traders to supply digital content/service in accordance with the contract and consumer’s reasonable expectations.

Discontinuation of the supply by the trader sooner than what was contractually agreed or what the consumer may reasonably expect would constitute a lack of conformity with the contract. In such cases, the consumer can terminate the contract and receive a proportionate refund of the price paid in advance for the digital content/service.
The assessment of consumer’s reasonable expectations is carried out on case-by-case basis.

While a new legislative initiative on this issue is not envisaged, in response to the European Citizens’ Initiative ‘Stop Destroying Videogames’2, the Commission intends to initiate stakeholder exchanges by the end of 2026 to explore the possibility of elaborating a selfregulatory/industry-led code of conduct to improve the management of video games’ end-oflife and strengthen transparency to consumers.

The Commission will also present its report on the application of the DCD by the end of 2026, covering also its application to the discontinuation of digital content and services. The purchase of videogames and other digital products do not necessarily constitute a transfer of ownership. Modern video game distribution models are typically based on licensing.

Although their terms and conditions may differ between vendors, the licenses acquired are not perpetual, nor are they mandated by EU copyright or other IP laws. Such licensing conditions, including any termination provisions, constitute a legal agreement governing the use of the purchased videogame.
1 Directive (EU) 2019/770 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2019 on certain aspects

concerning contracts for the supply of digital content and digital services, OJ L 136, 22.5.2019, p. 1-27. 2 Communication from the commission on the European Citizens’ Initiative (ECI) Stop Destroying Videogames, C/2026/4110, OJ C, C/2026/3601, 9.7.2026.
